title: Ethical Analysis
body:
**Ethical analysis** is the procedure the course tests: take a concrete case, apply each
framework in turn, and report what each concludes and on what grounds. The frameworks disagree,
and the disagreement is the useful part, because it locates exactly what the argument is about.

```
Case: a company deploys a hiring model trained on ten years of its own hires.
      It performs well on average and rejects women at a higher rate.

Utilitarianism   the total: faster hiring, lower cost, better average fit,
                 against harm to a group and the cost of losing good candidates.
                 The answer depends on how the totals are weighed and who counts.

Kantianism       is the rule universalisable, and does it treat applicants as
                 ends? Judging an individual by a group statistic uses them as
                 an instrument for efficiency. Prohibited regardless of the total.

Social contract  would applicants have agreed to this process in advance,
                 knowing how it works? The answer decides whether the practice
                 is legitimate as well as profitable.
```

The three reach different conclusions from the same facts, which is why an ethical claim has to
name its standard. A structured analysis states the case, identifies the stakeholders, applies
each framework, and then argues for one, and skipping to the last step is what makes an
argument unconvincing.

The link to the technical courses is direct. The disparate rejection rate above is a
[[Confusion Matrix]] whose error rates differ across groups, which is a measurable
property, so the ethical question and the statistical one are answered with the same numbers.
